core: The working definition of insurance: a system in which many people pay premiums so the few who suffer covered losses get paid — anchored to NAIC's 'a way to manage your financial risks' and Investopedia's risk-pooling description

How it works: a policy is the contract; premiums keep it active; the policyholder usually pays a deductible when using the insurance; the insurer pays its share of covered losses; insurance only covers the specific events listed in the policy
The four core terms with one line and one original example each: premium, deductible, coverage limit, claim
The common personal insurance types named with one line each: auto, home/renters, health, life, disability (health-insurance-basics and life-insurance-basics are sibling topics that own the depth)
The deductible trade-off: higher deductibles generally mean lower premiums because the policyholder takes on more of each claim
What insurance is NOT: not savings, not an investment — premiums are the price of protection and are not returned when no claim is filed
The honest framing: insurance protects the life you have built (protection against unexpected financial costs and loss of assets, per Investopedia; the Protect principle of MyMoney.gov)
supporting: Risk-based pricing: premiums are set by the insurer's assessment of how likely you are to file a claim and the coverage you choose; more risk and more coverage usually mean a higher premium
How claims work for auto/home/renters: document the loss, report the event, complete a claim form; the insurer reviews and pays if the policy covers the event
Auto insurance is required in almost every state; lenders typically require it for financed or leased vehicles
outOfScope: Health insurance depth: plans, networks, copays, coinsurance, marketplaces (own sibling topic: personal-finance:foundations:health-insurance-basics)
Life insurance depth: term vs permanent, beneficiaries, cash value (own sibling topic: personal-finance:foundations:life-insurance-basics)

claims.claim: Insurance is a way to manage your financial risks: people buy it to protect themselves from unexpected costs, because recovering from disasters and medical emergencies can cost a lot, and insurance helps them avoid paying the entire cost of treatment, services, repairs, and rebuilds on their own.

Insurance works through a contract called a policy: under the policy you agree to pay a premium, you usually pay a deductible when you use the insurance, and the company agrees to pay its share of the cost for covered losses or events; insurance only covers the specific events listed in the policy.
An insurance company pools clients' risks to make payments more affordable for the insured: many people pay premiums so the few who suffer covered losses can be paid.

A premium is the regular payment you make to keep coverage active, regardless of whether you file a claim; it is the price of a policy, set through underwriting, and more risk and more coverage usually mean a higher premium.

A deductible is the dollar amount of a claim you pay yourself before the insurance company pays its share; deductibles deter large volumes of small claims, and policies with higher deductibles are typically less expensive.

A coverage limit (policy limit) is the maximum amount an insurer will pay for a covered loss under a policy; limits may apply per claim, per period, or over the life of the policy, and higher limits typically carry higher premiums.

A claim is a request asking your insurer to pay its share of the bill for a covered event or service; for auto, home, and renters insurance, the policyholder typically documents the loss, reports the event, completes a claim form, and the insurer reviews it and pays if the policy covers the event.

Common personal insurance types include auto, health, homeowners, renters, life, and disability; auto insurance is required in almost every state; homeowners and renters policies protect the home, belongings, and liability against damage, theft, and disasters, with renters coverage protecting belongings rather than the building; disability insurance replaces a portion of income when an individual is unable to work due to a disabling condition.

Insurance is protection, not savings or an investment: premiums are paid to keep coverage active whether or not a claim is filed and are not returned if nothing happens, and the payment, if any, is tied to a covered loss rather than to growth of the money paid in.

Federal money guidance (MyMoney.gov) treats insurance as part of protecting your financial situation — accumulating emergency savings and buying insurance — and Investopedia summarizes that insurance helps protect you and your family against unexpected financial costs, resulting debts, and the risk of losing your assets.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does a higher deductible always mean a lower premium?
positions: Investopedia: policies with high deductibles are typically less expensive because the higher out-of-pocket expense results in fewer small claims.
NAIC: 'more risk and more coverage usually mean a higher premium' — coverage and risk raise price; the deductible shifts cost between the premium and the out-of-pocket share.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the trade-off as a general relationship (higher deductible → lower premium for otherwise similar coverage), not as a guarantee for any specific quote; premiums are set case by case through underwriting.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is insurance ever a savings or investment vehicle?
positions: This lesson: ordinary insurance premiums buy protection and are not a savings balance or an investment return.
Investopedia notes that some permanent life insurance policies can build cash value over time.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Life-insurance products that build cash value are owned by the life-insurance-basics sibling topic; this foundations lesson states the general-purpose distinction (premiums are not returned, payments are tied to covered losses) and links to that topic.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No generated draft claims were carried over; the lesson was written from verified sources only.
